record.paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
record.original_question: Do some manganites exhibit two genuinely different mechanisms for colossal magnetoresistance, one associated with the standard transition into a ferromagnetic metal near higher temperature and another associated with a low-temperature first-order field-induced metal-insulator transition, and can theory explain both within a unified phase-competition framework?

evidence.quote: Is this indicative of two independent mechanisms for CMR?
Can theory explain the presence of two types of CMR transitions? The answer is tentatively yes, although more work is needed to confirm the picture.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider hole-doped manganite perovskites of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a rare-earth and A an alkaline-earth cation), modeled by competing ferromagnetic metallic (FM) and charge/orbital-ordered insulating (CO/OO) phases, with degrees of freedom including itinerant e_g electrons coupled via double-exchange to localized t_{2g} spins, Jahn–Teller phonons, and superexchange antiferromagnetic interactions. Experimentally, some such compounds display two distinct colossal magnetoresistance (CMR) regimes as functions of temperature T and applied magnetic field H:

(a) a high-temperature CMR near the paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic-metal transition at T = T_C, where resistivity drops continuously with field; and

(b) a low-temperature CMR associated with a first-order, field-induced metal–insulator transition out of a charge/orbital-ordered (or otherwise insulating) state, exhibiting hysteresis as a function of H.

Question: Do these two CMR regimes correspond to genuinely distinct physical mechanisms, and can a single theoretical framework based on phase competition and intrinsic inhomogeneity (electronic phase separation between FM-metallic and insulating phases on nanometer-to-mesoscopic scales, with percolation-type transport) account for both (a) and (b) simultaneously, including the qualitative dependence of the two CMR signatures on temperature, magnetic field, bandwidth, and quenched disorder?
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent theoretical and experimental work supports a phase-competition / electronic phase-separation picture in which both the high-T CMR near T_C and the low-T field-induced first-order metal-insulator transition in CO/OO manganites arise from competition between FM-metallic and insulating phases, with quenched disorder enabling nanoscale coexistence and percolative transport. A fully unified, quantitative microscopic theory covering both regimes across all relevant manganite families is not established, so the question is best characterized as partially resolved.

status_evidence.title: Origin of colossal magnetoresistance in LaMnO3 manganite
status_evidence.snippet: Double-exchange and Jahn-Teller interplay captures essence at atomic level; phase competition dominates at nanoscale.
status_evidence.claim: Two complementary mechanisms (double-exchange/JT and phase competition) are needed to describe CMR.

status_evidence.title: Multi-Scale Phase Modulations in Colossal Magnetoresistance Manganites
status_evidence.snippet: Phase coexistence and competition between FM metallic and CO insulating phases underlies CMR across temperature and field.
status_evidence.claim: Phase-competition framework unifies high-T and low-T CMR signatures.

status_evidence.title: Factors affecting resistivity and CMR of manganite materials
status_evidence.snippet: Magnetic field induces PM-FM, metal-insulator, and structural transitions in CMR perovskites near T_C, with disorder-mediated inhomogeneity essential.
status_evidence.claim: Field-induced first-order MI transitions are an established companion mechanism to the standard T_C CMR.
